name: render-props
intent: Let a component hand its own state to a caller-supplied function-valued prop and render whatever that function returns, so one piece of behaviour serves many appearances while every call site keeps control of the markup.
problem: A component owns reusable state or behaviour - a subscription, form state, list data, animation values - but its output is hard-wired to one markup structure, so consumers that need different markup must copy the logic, wrap and patch the component, or bend their design around the shipped DOM. The recurring decision is how a stateful component can expose its state to an unknown call site without dictating what that call site renders.
context: Component-based UI codebases where the reuse mechanism can pass a function into a component and the framework re-renders the call site when the owner's state changes: React/Vue props and scoped slots, Blazor templated components, Compose and SwiftUI composable closures, WPF data templates, and toolkit cell/renderer factories. It applies when the owner must keep the behaviour - lifecycle, subscriptions, context, refs, portals - while the consumer owns structure and styling; it is largely superseded by hooks and composables when only logic or state is shared.
benefits: One behaviour, many appearances: the owner ships no markup, so every consumer renders the state with its own elements, styling solution and design system instead of restyling someone else's DOM.

Data arrives as explicit function arguments rather than a merged prop bag, so the call site sees exactly which values the owner provides - the naming-collision and precedence problems that plague higher-order components do not arise.

Composition without inheritance: several function-valued props give a typed slot API (renderItem, renderHeader, renderEmpty), and generic owners serve any item type with the state type inferred at the call site.
Works where a hook cannot: the owner can own a subtree - a provider, refs, portals, an animated presence - and still let the consumer author the markup inside it.
Adoption is incremental: the owner can be introduced around existing markup, and a later conversion to a hook or a design-system component does not rewrite the consumers' rendering decisions.
tradeoffs: Callback pyramids: nesting several owner components to combine multiple data sources reads far worse than flat hook calls, and the nesting depth grows with every source added.

Per-render function values defeat memoization: an inline render prop is a new value on every parent render, so memo-style short-circuits around the owner stop working in tight paths, and the extra ownership boundary is an extra node in the tree.
Rendering decisions scatter across call sites: loading, empty and error branches must be re-decided by every consumer because the owner deliberately has no rendering opinions.

Superseded for pure logic reuse: where the framework has hooks or composables the same result is reached with fewer indirections, and libraries have migrated their primary APIs (Apollo, React Router, Formik) while keeping the component form for compatibility.
A function-valued children prop is invisible at the type level by default: consumers who pass nodes where a function is expected fail at render time unless the owner documents and types the contract.

participants.responsibility: Owns the state, effects and lifecycle; calls the function-valued prop with the current state instead of implementing its own render logic.
Maps the state the owner passes into markup; the only place where structure and styling are decided.
Supplies the function, receives the state as arguments, and composes the returned markup into its own tree.
Provides the prop/slot mechanism, re-renders the owner when state changes, and places the consumer's markup in the tree.

use_cases: Headless component libraries that ship behaviour with consumer markup (Downshift's render-prop form, React Aria builders, TanStack Table).
Drag-and-drop and other wrappers that must own a subtree boundary - context, refs or portals - while the consumer authors the children (react-beautiful-dnd's provided/snapshot arguments).
Animation primitives that thread interpolated values into consumer markup every frame (Framer Motion, React Spring).
List and table renderers with per-slot functions such as renderItem, renderEmpty and ListHeaderComponent - the shape React Native's FlatList popularised.
Cross-cutting state such as mouse position, geolocation or form validation shared by screens that each display it differently.
Pre-hooks data fetching components (Apollo Query/Mutation) retained for consumers that cannot use hooks.
Downshift's <Downshift> children function exposes combobox state and prop getters while rendering no UI, so consumers can build custom accessible autocomplete markup.
react-beautiful-dnd's <Droppable> and <Draggable> function children pass refs, required props and drag snapshots while the consumer controls each draggable element's structure and styling.
React Motion's <Motion> children function receives interpolated style values on each animation frame, allowing those values to drive arbitrary consumer markup.
avoid_when: Only logic or state is shared and the owner would just call props.children(data): use a custom hook or composable, which adds no tree node and no indirection.
The consumer always renders the same output: a normal component with ordinary props is simpler.
Several data sources must be combined in one component: prefer hooks/composables and pass the state down, to avoid the render-prop pyramid.
The framework's slot or template mechanism is the idiomatic way to hand markup to a component (Vue slots, Blazor templates, SwiftUI view content) and no function prop is needed.
State should be shared by many unrelated consumers: context/provider or a store is the right mechanism, not a per-call render function.
anti_patterns: A wrapper whose entire body is return props.children(data): indirection that adds a tree node without adding capability.
Inline render props in hot paths, defeating memoization and re-rendering heavy subtrees on every parent render.
Undocumented function-as-children: consumers pass a node where a function is expected and the component fails at render time.
Using the render callback for side effects or expensive pull-based work instead of exposing the state for the consumer to use.
Render props stacked with prop-merging wrappers, recreating the naming collisions and merge-order bugs the pattern exists to avoid.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: behaviour and lifecycle live in the owner; presentation is entirely the consumer's.
Inversion of control (Hollywood principle): the owner calls the consumer's function, not the other way round.
Composition over inheritance: reuse is parameterisation with functions, not subclassing or wrapper inheritance chains.
Explicit dependencies: state crosses the boundary as function arguments, so the data flow is visible at the call site.
Single responsibility: one unit owns state, the other decides how it looks.
best_practices: Name the function prop for its job (renderItem, renderEmpty, renderHeader) and document that children may be a function where that spelling exists.
Type the function prop precisely - a generic RenderProp<T> alias - so the state arguments are inferred at every call site.
Keep the owner free of markup and side effects: pass state in and let the consumer decide everything visual.
Stabilise the function in hot paths (memoization, a stable child, or the framework compiler) before blaming the pattern for re-render cost.
Model loading, error and empty states in the state value the owner passes, so every consumer only has to decorate them.

Prefer the framework's slot/template mechanism where it is the platform's idiomatic way to hand markup to a component; reserve raw function props for APIs that must stay framework-agnostic or serve non-hook consumers.
sources: Michael Jackson, 'Use a Render Prop!' (2017) - the article the React documentation credits with the term's origin.
React Motion repository, Motion render-prop API: https://github.com/chenglou/react-motion/blob/master/README.md
Dmitri Pavlutin, 'How to Solve React Render Props Callback Hell': https://dmitripavlutin.com/solve-react-render-props-callback-hell/
